title: Celsus names no prophecy
source_text: Ὅτι δὲ καὶ Χριστιανῶν τινες καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι, οἱ μὲν καταβεβηκέναι (λέγουσιν,) οἱ δὲ καταβήσεσθαι εἰς τὴν γῆν τινα θεὸν ἢ θεοῦ υἱὸν τῶν τῇδε δικαιωτὴν, τοῦτ᾿ αἴσχιστον, καὶ οὐδὲ δεῖται μακροῦ λόγου ὁ ἔλεγχος. καὶ δοκεῖ γε ἀκριβῶς περὶ μὲν Ἰουδαίων οὐ τινῶν ἀλλὰ πάντων λέγειν ὅτι οἴονταί τινα καταβήσεσθαι ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, περὶ δὲ Χριστιανῶν οτι τινὲς αὐτῶν καταβεβηκέναι λέγουσιν. ἐμφαίνει γὰρ τοὺς ἀπὸ Ἰουδαϊκῶν γραφῶν κατασκευάζοντας τὴν Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημίαν ὡς ἤδη γεγενημένην, καὶ ἔοικεν εἰδέναι ὅτι εἰσί τινες αἱρέσεις ἀρνούμεναι Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν εἶναι τὸν πεπροφητευμένον. ἤδη μὲν οὖν καὶ ἐν τοῖς προτέροις περὶ τοῦ πεπροφητεῦσθαι τὸν Χριστὸν κατὰ δύναμιν διειλήφαμεν, διὸ τὰ πολλὰ τῶν δυναμένων λέγεσθαι εἰς τὸν τόπον οὐκ ἐπαναλαμβάνομεν, ἵνα μὴ παλιλλογῶμεν. ὅρα δὴ ὅτι, εἴπερ μετά τινος κἂν δοκούσης ἀκολουθίας ἐβούλετο ἀνατρέπειν τὴν περὶ τῶν προφητειῶν (ἢ) περὶ τοῦ ἐπιδημήσειν ἢ ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τὸν Χριστὸν πίστιν, ἐχρῆν αὐτὸν αὐτὰς ἐκθέσθαι τὰς προφητείας. αἷς ἐν τῷ διαλέγεσθαι πρὸς ἀλλήλους χρώμεθα Χριστιανοὶ καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι· οὕτως γὰρ ἂν κἂν ἔδοξε τοὺς περισπωμένους ὑπὸ τῆς, ὡς οἴεται, πιθανότητος [δοκεῖν] ἀνατρέπειν ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς τὰ προφητικὰ συγκαταθέσεως καὶ τῆς διὰ τὰ προφητικὰ εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὡς ὄντα Χριστὸν πίστεως· νυνὶ δὲ ἤτοι μὴ δυνάμενος ἀπαντῆσαι πρὸς τὰς περὶ Χριστοῦ προφητείας (ἢ) μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς, τίνα ἐστὶ τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ προφητευόμενα, οὐδεμίαν μὲν λέξιν τίθησι προφητικὴν, καίτοι γε μυρίαι ὅσαι εἰσὶ περὶ Χριστοῦ, κατηγορεῖν δὲ οἴεται τῶν προφητικῶν, μηδ᾿ ἣν εἴποι ἂν ἐκεῖνος πιθανότητα αὐτῶν ἐκθέμενος. οὐκ οἶδε μέντοι γε ὅτι οὐ πάνυ τι Ἰουδαῖοι λέγουσι θεὸν ὄντα τὸν Χριστὸν καταβήσεσθαι ἢ θεοῦ υἱὸν, ὡς καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν.
pass_a_gloss: [Celsus:] 'That both some of Christians and Jews, the ones [say] (λέγουσιν, editorial supplement) to have come down (καταβαίνω, perf. inf.), the others to be going to come down (fut. inf.) to the earth, some god (θεός) or son of god (θεοῦ υἱός) as judge/setter-right (δικαιωτής) of the things here (τῶν τῇδε), this is most shameful (αἴσχιστος), and the refutation (ἔλεγχος) does not even need a long argument (λόγος).' And he seems indeed to speak precisely (ἀκριβῶς): about Jews, not some but all, that they think (οἴομαι) someone will come down onto the earth, but about Christians that some of them say [he] has come down. For he indicates (ἐμφαίνω) those establishing (κατασκευάζω) from Jewish Scriptures (γραφαί) the coming (ἐπιδημία) of Christ as already having happened, and he seems to know that there are some sects/parties (αἱρέσεις) denying that Christ Jesus is the one prophesied (προφητεύω). Already in the earlier [books] we have discussed (διαλαμβάνω) according to power (κατὰ δύναμιν) about Christ having been prophesied; therefore we do not take up again (ἐπαναλαμβάνω) most of the things able to be said on the topic (τόπος), so as not to repeat (παλιλλογέω). See (ὁράω) then that, if with some even seeming (δοκέω) logical sequence (ἀκολουθία) he wished to overturn (ἀνατρέπω) the faith (πίστις) about the prophecies (προφητεῖαι) [or] (supplement) about Christ's being going to come (ἐπιδημέω) or having come, he ought (χρή) to have set out (ἐκτίθημι) the prophecies themselves, which we Christians and Jews use in debating (διαλέγομαι) with one another; for thus he might at least have seemed to turn away (ἀνατρέπω) those drawn about (περισπάω) by the, as he thinks, persuasiveness (πιθανότης) from their assent (συγκατάθεσις) to the prophetic [writings] and from the faith through the prophetic [writings] in Jesus as being Christ. But now, either not being able to meet (ἀπαντάω) the prophecies about Christ [or] (supplement) not even at all (τὴν ἀρχήν) knowing what are the things prophesied about him, he puts (τίθημι) no prophetic saying (λέξις), although there are countless (μυρίαι ὅσαι) about Christ, but he thinks to accuse (κατηγορέω) the prophetic [writings], not even setting out what he would call their persuasiveness. He does not know, however, that Jews do not at all say that Christ, being God, will come down, or [as] Son of God, as we have also said above (ἀνωτέρω).
pass_b_english: “That some of the Christians, and the Jews, say, the former that some god or son of a god has come down to the earth as judge of the things here, the latter that he will come down, is most shameful, and its refutation does not even need a long argument.”

And here he does seem to speak with precision. Of the Jews he says, not of some but of all, that they think someone will come down to the earth; but of the Christians, that some of them say he has come down. For he is pointing to those who show from the Jewish Scriptures that the coming of Christ has already taken place, and he seems to know that there are some sects which deny that Christ Jesus is the one who was prophesied.

We have already treated in the earlier books, as far as we were able, the fact that Christ was prophesied; so we do not take up again most of what could be said on the subject, so as not to repeat ourselves. But notice this: if he wanted, with an argument that at least seemed to hold together, to overturn faith in the prophecies, or faith that Christ will come or has come, he ought to have set out the very prophecies that we Christians and Jews use when we debate with each other. In that way he might at least have seemed to draw those who are swayed by their persuasiveness, as he regards it, away from their assent to the prophetic writings and from the faith in Jesus as the Christ that comes to them through those writings.

As it is, either because he cannot answer the prophecies about Christ, or because he does not even know in the first place what the things prophesied about him are, he sets down not a single prophetic saying, though there are countless ones about Christ; and yet he thinks he can accuse the prophetic writings without even setting out what he himself would call their persuasiveness. He does not know, however, that the Jews by no means say that the Christ will come down as God, or as Son of God, as we have also said above.

choices.choice: ‘with even a show of reasoned sequence’ → ‘with an argument that at least seemed to hold together’ (calque of μετά τινος κἂν δοκούσης ἀκολουθίας)
‘And he does seem to speak precisely here’ → ‘And here he does seem to speak with precision’
Confirmed speaker split: opening sentence is Celsus (quoted), the rest is Origen; οἱ μέν/οἱ δέ = Christians/Jews kept

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 2 (Koetschau 4.2). The opening sentence is Celsus’s own wording, introduced by φησίν at the end of 4.1, so it is set in quotation marks. Koetschau’s supplement (λέγουσιν) and the two supplied (ἢ) are accepted; the bracketed [δοκεῖν] is an editorial deletion and is not translated. In Celsus’s sentence οἱ μέν refers to the Christians and οἱ δέ to the Jews; Origen’s next comment turns on τινες attaching only to the Christians, so the English keeps ‘some of the Christians, and the Jews’. Celsus speaks generically of ‘some god or son of a god’, so these stay lower case; in Origen’s last sentence the titles refer to Christ and are capitalised. δικαιωτής rendered ‘judge’ (one who sets right or passes sentence); compare δικαιῶσαι in 4.7. ‘As he regards it’ renders ὡς οἴεται, marking the persuasiveness as Celsus’s view of the prophecies. ‘As we have also said above’ refers back to earlier discussion of Jewish expectation; not pinned to a section here. No Scripture quoted.
